title: Of a saying of Caesar
paragraphs: If we would sometimes spend a little thought on ourselves, and use the time we waste prying into other men's actions and into things outside us to examine our own capacities instead, we would soon see what frail and decaying material this fabric of ours is made of. Is it not a striking proof of our imperfection that we cannot settle our satisfaction on any one thing, and that even our own fancy and desire rob us of the power to choose what is most fitting and useful for us? A good demonstration is the unending dispute among the philosophers about finding man's sovereign good — a dispute still going and likely to go on forever, with no solution and no agreement.
"Dum abest quod avemus, id exsuperare videtur Caetera; post aliud, quum contigit illud, avemus, Et sitis aequa tenet."
["While the thing we want is missing, it seems to surpass everything else; then, once we have it, we want something else, and the same thirst keeps hold of us." — Lucretius, iii. 1095.]

Whatever falls into our knowledge and our possession, we find it does not satisfy, and we keep panting after things to come and unknown — since what is present does not suffice us. Not, in my judgement, that they lack what would do the job, but because we lay hold of them with an unruly and immoderate haste:

"Nam quum vidit hic, ad victum qux flagitat usus, Et per quae possent vitam consistere tutam, Omnia jam ferme mortalibus esse parata; Divitiis homines, et honore, et laude potentes Aflluere, atque bona natorum excellere fama; Nec minus esse domi cuiquam tamen anxia corda, Atque animi ingratis vitam vexare querelis Causam, quae infestis cogit saevire querelis, Intellegit ibi; vitium vas efficere ipsum, Omniaque, illius vitio, corrumpier intus, Qux collata foris et commoda quomque venirent."

["For when he saw that nearly everything required for survival, and everything that could make life secure, is already laid out for mortals' hands — that men have abundant wealth, honour, praise, and the joy of children with a good name, and yet for all that no one's heart at home is free of anxieties, his mind worn down by ungrateful complaints — he understood that the vessel itself was at fault, and that all the good things brought into it from outside were spoiled by its own defects." — Lucretius, vi. 9.]

Our appetite is unsteady and fickle; it can neither hold nor enjoy anything with any grace. Man, deciding the fault lies with the things he possesses, fills himself with — and feeds on — the idea of things he neither knows nor understands; on these he hangs his hopes and his desires, paying them all reverence and honour, in the spirit of Caesar's saying:
"Communi fit vitio naturae, ut invisis, latitantibus atque incognitis rebus magis confidamas, vehementiusque exterreamur."
["It is the common vice of nature that we put the most trust in, and feel the greatest fear of, things unseen, hidden, and unknown." — De Bello Civili, xi. 4.]
